items.title: The Prose Commentary Opens: Two Extremes to Avoid, and What "Agent" Actually Means

items.zh: 此中依止補特伽羅無我勝義，宣說如是勝義伽他。為欲對治增益、損減二邊執故。
items.en: Resting on the ultimate truth of the selflessness of persons, these ultimate-meaning verses are taught, in order to counteract two extreme attachments: the extreme of over-imputation, and the extreme of under-imputation.

items.zh: 於所攝受說為宰主，於諸業用說為作者，於諸果報說為受者。如是半頌，遮遣別義所分別我。諸法亦無用者，遮遣即法所分別我。由此遠離增益邊執。而用轉非無者，顯法有性。由此遠離損減邊執。
items.en: Regarding what is taken up, one speaks of a "ruler"; regarding the various functions of karma, one speaks of an "agent"; regarding results, one speaks of an "experiencer." This much refutes the imagined self conceived as separate from the aggregates. "The constituents have no such function of their own" refutes the imagined self conceived as identical with the aggregates. By this, the extreme of over-imputation is abandoned. "Yet the functioning that occurs is not simply nothing" reveals that phenomena genuinely have a nature. By this, the extreme of under-imputation is abandoned.

items.zh: 用有三種。一、宰主用，二、作者用，三、受者用。因此用故，假立宰主、作者、受者。雖言諸法，而未宣說何等為法，故次說言唯有十二支等半頌。如有支次第，諸蘊等流轉，此顯不取微細多我，便能對治宰主、作者及受者執。眼色為緣，生眼識果，無別受者。此中顯示，即十八界說受者性。雖言無主，而未宣說無何等主，為欲顯示，故次說言：審思此一切，眾生不可得。言審思者，由依三量審諦觀察。此若無者，云何建立內外成就？故次說言：於內及於外，是一切皆空。此顯內外唯假建立。云何建立能觀、所觀二種成就？故次說言：其能修空者，亦常無所有。云何建立聖者、異生二種成就？故次說言：我我定非有，由顛倒妄計。此顯聖者及異生我，決定無有真實我性，唯由顛倒妄計為有。云何建立彼此成就？故次說言：有情我皆無。云何建立染淨成就？故次說言：唯有因法有。染者、淨者、皆不可得。雖說諸法皆無作用、而未宣說云何無用，故次說言：諸行皆剎那，住尚無況用。如前已說用轉非無。云何無用而有用轉？故次說言：即說彼生起，為用為作者。果故，名為用；因故，名作者。彼生起者，顯從諸處諸識得生。彼得生者，非離眼等彼成就故。如前所說諸法無用，此顯無用略有七種。一、無作用用。謂眼不能見色等。二、無隨轉用。謂於此亦無能任持、驅役者。如其次第，宰主、作者，俱無所有，故無有能隨轉作用。三、無生他用。謂法不能生他。四、無自生用。謂亦不能自生。五、無移轉用。謂眾緣有故生，非故新新有。六、無滅他用。謂法不能滅他。七、無自滅用。謂亦不能自滅。問：如眾緣有故生，亦眾緣有故滅耶？答：眾緣有故生，生已自然滅。如前所說有因法有，欲顯在家及與出家雜染自性有因法有。故次說言：由二品為依，是生便可得等。由此二頌，顯無明、愛有因法有。次後五頌，顯雜染品差別所依因及時分。此中，「有因諸法」者，謂無明乃至受。有因眾苦者，謂愛乃至老死。此言顯示煩惱、業、生三種雜染。「根本二惑故」者，此言顯示煩惱雜染，唯取最勝煩惱雜染。「自無能作用」等言，復重別顯業雜染義。由彼所作有差別故，彼果異熟不思議故。「
items.en: Function is of three kinds: first, the function of a ruler; second, the function of an agent; third, the function of an experiencer. Because of these functions, a ruler, an agent, and an experiencer are provisionally designated. Although 'dharmas' has been mentioned, it has not yet been said which dharmas are meant, so the next half-verse says, 'only the twelve links', and so on. 'As the links follow in order, the aggregates and the rest flow on': this shows that one does not take there to be many subtle selves, and so it counteracts clinging to a ruler, an agent, and an experiencer. With the eye and form as conditions, the result, eye-consciousness, arises, and there is no separate experiencer: this shows that the eighteen elements themselves are what is called the experiencer. Although it has been said that there is no ruler, it has not yet been said what kind of ruler there is not; to show this, the next line says, 'Examining all this carefully, no being can be found.' 'Examining carefully' means investigating closely by relying on the three means of knowledge. If there is no such being, how are inner and outer established? So the next line says, 'Within and without, all this is empty.' This shows that inner and outer are only provisionally established. How are the two, the one who contemplates and what is contemplated, established? So the next line says, 'The one who cultivates emptiness is also, always, nothing at all.' How are the two, noble ones and ordinary beings, established? So the next line says, 'The self is certainly not existent; it is falsely imagined through inversion.' This shows that the self of noble ones and of ordinary beings certainly has no real self-nature and is only falsely imagined to exist through inversion. How are 'this' and 'that' established? So the next line says, 'Beings and selves are all non-existent.' How are the defiled and the purified established? So the next line says, 'Only dharmas with causes exist.' The one who is defiled and the one who is purified cannot be found. Although it has been said that all dharmas lack function, it has not yet been said in what way they lack function, so the next line says, 'All formations are momentary; they do not even abide, still less function.' As said before, the working of function is not absent. How can function work where there is no function? So the next line says, 'Their arising itself is called function and is called agent.' As result it is called function; as cause it is called agent. 'Their arising' shows that consciousnesses arise from the various sense bases. Their arising is not established apart from the eye and the rest. The lack of function in dharmas spoken of earlier is, in brief, of seven kinds. First, no function of activity: the eye cannot see forms and so on. Second, no function of directing: here there is nothing that holds or drives; in order, a ruler and an agent are both absent, so there is no function of directing. Third, no function of producing another: a dharma cannot produce another. Fourth, no function of producing itself: nor can it produce itself. Fifth, no function of transferring: things arise because conditions are present, newly each time, not carried over. Sixth, no function of destroying another: a dharma cannot destroy another. Seventh, no function of destroying itself: nor can it destroy itself. Question: As things arise because conditions are present, do they also cease because conditions are present? Answer: They arise because conditions are present; having arisen, they cease of themselves. It was said above that dharmas with causes exist; to show that the defilement of householders and renunciants alike is by nature a dharma with causes, the next line says, 'Based on the two classes, it is found as soon as there is birth', and so on. These two verses show that ignorance and craving exist as dharmas with causes. The next five verses show the distinctions of the defiled class, its supports, its causes, and its timing. Here, 'dharmas with causes' means ignorance through feeling; 'sufferings with causes' means craving through old age and death. This shows the three kinds of defilement: of affliction, of karma, and of birth. 'Because of the two root afflictions' shows the defilement of affliction, taking only its strongest form. The words 'it has no power of its own to act', and so on, show separately once more the meaning of karmic defilement: because what is done differs, and because the ripening of its result is inconceivable.

blocks.text: From today, the treatise explains the forty-four verses in prose. **Most of this prose is missing from Ru-Yi's translation** (0364a24–c12 today; most of the next two days as well), so the English column gives our own translation, marked as ours. The commentary below also summarises it section by section, to help you follow the argument.

(Translated.) The verses rest on the non-self of persons in the ultimate sense, and counter two extremes: **superimposition** (adding a self that is not there) and **detraction** (denying what does exist). The first half-verse rejects a self as "ruler" over what one possesses, as "agent" of actions, and as "experiencer" of results. "Dharmas have no function" rejects even a self imagined in the dharmas themselves. "Yet functioning is not absent" affirms that dharmas do exist as processes; this avoids detraction.

items: **Three functions.** There are three "functions" (用): of ruling, of acting, and of experiencing. Because these functions occur, a ruler, agent, and experiencer are provisionally designated.

**What the dharmas are.** The verse says "only the twelve links" to specify which dharmas are meant. Showing that the links flow on as aggregates without "a subtle plurality of selves" counters the notions of ruler, agent, and experiencer. "With the eye and form as conditions, eye-consciousness arises as result; there is no separate experiencer": the eighteen elements themselves are what we call the experiencer.

**Examining carefully.** "Examining all this, no being can be found": examined by the three means of knowledge (Days 119–121), inner and outer are both empty, merely designated. Even "one who cultivates emptiness" is not a real self. Noble ones and ordinary beings alike have no real self; ordinary beings only imagine one through inversion. "Only dharmas with causes exist": the defiled and the purified person cannot be found.

**Why no function.** "All formations are momentary; they do not even abide, still less act." Yet the verse said functioning is not absent: their arising is called "function" from the side of result, and "agent" from the side of cause.

**Seven absences of function.** The prose lists them: (1) the eye does not "see" as an agent; (2) there is no controller or driver; (3) a dharma cannot produce another; (4) nor produce itself; (5) nothing transfers from moment to moment: things arise anew from conditions; (6) a dharma cannot destroy another; (7) nor destroy itself. Asked whether things cease because of conditions as they arise because of conditions, the answer is: "arising needs conditions; having arisen, it ceases of itself."

blocks.text: The argument is the Yogācāra form of the Buddha's teaching that there is "action, but no actor". Processes occur, and we name agents to talk about them. The danger on one side is believing in a hidden self; on the other, concluding that nothing happens at all. Both teachers return to this balance often: no self, yet karma and its results continue.

quiz.q: The prose says the verses counter the extremes of over- and under-imputation. How does Venerable Miào Jìng define over-imputation?
options: clinging to a self where there is none — adding something
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "There is no self at all, yet one clings to a self — that is over-imputation; it adds." "The functioning is not nothing" shows phenomena have a nature, avoiding under-imputation.

quiz.q: The English adds "provisionally" to "ruler, agent, experiencer," reading them as allowed conventions. How does Venerable Miào Jìng read this half-verse?
options: these lines name the "self conceived apart from the aggregates" to be refuted; the true provisional designations come later, in "function has three kinds"
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Clinging to a self apart from form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness — that is 'a self conceived as something separate.'" The half-verse refutes it.

quiz.q: How does Venerable Miào Jìng describe the 宰 of 宰主, "ruler"?
options: I give the order — tell you to do this, you do it; tell you that, you do it
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "I give orders — tell you to be like this, you are; like that, you are — that is 宰." Later he defines the provisional ruler as deciding, the agent as acting, the experiencer as enjoying results.

quiz.q: "The constituents have no function" refutes the self identical with the aggregates. What does it mean, per Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: not that dharmas lack function, but that they lack the function of a self — the view that the aggregates are the self is also wrong
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: some non-Buddhists take the aggregates as the self — also wrong, because "dharmas have no function": not that they lack function, but that they lack a self's function.

quiz.q: "The functioning is not nothing" reveals that phenomena have a nature. What does Master Cháng Bǎi criticise with it?
options: the wrong grasp of emptiness — one can't deny everything; denying all may lead to not practising; overclinging to emptiness is wrong too
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "One can't deny everything; denying everything is the wrong grasp of emptiness, and may lead to not practising — overdoing emptiness is wrong too." This avoids under-imputation.
